lessons.title: SEBI's Fairness Rules — Cable Length, Randomization, and the NSE Co-lo Case

children.text: Every firm in NSE's colocation facility is paying the same posted fee for the same nominal service. That should mean they are all equally fast. For several years in the mid-2010s, Indian regulators found that was not quite true, and the resulting case became one of the defining episodes in how SEBI thinks about fairness inside a colocation facility.
The Problem: Not All Colocated Racks Are Equal

The previous lesson treated colocation as something anyone could buy. That is true, but it created a second, subtler fairness question once inside the facility: are all colocated members actually equal to each other? A rack placed slightly closer to the exchange's core switch, a cable a few metres shorter, or a server assigned to a marginally faster secondary node can hand one colocated firm a real, persistent advantage over another colocated firm, even though both are paying the same fees for the same nominal service.

body.title: The NSE Co-location Case: A Timeline

events.title: A whistleblower complaint
events.description: An anonymous complaint alleged that NSE's system for assigning colocated members to its tick-by-tick data dissemination servers was not truly randomized, letting whichever member's server connected first to a given secondary server keep a persistent speed edge.

events.title: SEBI opens an investigation
events.description: SEBI examined how NSE's co-location architecture allocated members across dissemination servers, and whether specific brokers, most notably OPG Securities, had exploited the design to gain a consistent, non-random latency advantage over other colocated firms.

events.title: Findings and enforcement action
events.description: SEBI's proceedings found that NSE had failed to ensure equal access among its own colocated members, and directed disgorgement of wrongful gains from the brokers found to have benefited, alongside scrutiny of NSE itself. Multiple parties, including NSE, contested aspects of these orders before the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT).

events.title: Remedial changes
events.description: Exchanges strengthened randomization in how colocated members are allocated to servers and racks, and SEBI's broader framework pushed toward giving all trading members, not just colocated ones, access to tick-by-tick data feeds, narrowing one source of information asymmetry.

body.text: The summary above captures the widely reported substance of the case. Specific dates, monetary figures, and the current status of any appeals should be checked against SEBI's and SAT's published orders directly, since regulatory proceedings of this kind span several years and multiple stages.

body.label: Core Regulatory Principle
body.context: SEBI's fairness framework for colocation is not about whether colocation itself is fair to non-colocated firms, that was the previous lesson's question. It is about ensuring firms that do pay for colocation cannot gain an unintended edge over each other through rack placement or server allocation.

body.title: Name the actual concern
body.textWithBlank: In the NSE co-location case, the core regulatory concern was that some brokers gained a persistent latency edge over other ___ members, not over firms outside the facility entirely.
body.explanation: The issue was fairness within the group of firms that had already paid for colocation, not fairness between colocated and non-colocated firms, which is a separate, already-settled question covered in the previous lesson.

body.text: Paying for colocation buys you into a room. SEBI's fairness rules exist to make sure everyone in that room is actually standing at the same distance from the finish line.

points: Colocation fairness has two separate layers: whether colocation itself is open to all who pay (previous lesson), and whether firms that do colocate are treated equally within the facility (this lesson).

The NSE co-location case centered on allegations that a flawed server allocation architecture let specific brokers, most notably OPG Securities, gain a persistent, non-random latency edge over other colocated members.

SEBI's investigation and enforcement action, along with Securities Appellate Tribunal proceedings, ran over several years and pushed exchanges toward randomized allocation of colocated members to servers and racks.
A related reform was widening access to tick-by-tick data feeds beyond just colocated members, reducing one source of information asymmetry.
Treat the specific dates and figures in this case as a starting point, not a final citation. Check SEBI's and SAT's published orders directly for the authoritative record.
